concept.name: WebSocket Real-Time Scaling

relationships.description: Connects WebSocket Real-Time Scaling to api gateway in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: WebSockets (RFC 6455) upgrade an HTTP connection into a persistent, full-duplex TCP frame stream; scaling to millions of concurrent connections shifts the bottleneck from request/sec to stateful memory, ephemeral ports, pub/sub fan-out, and reconnect storms.
spark.keyTakeaway: Terminate TLS and WebSockets on stateless L4-balanced connection gateways backed by a sharded pub/sub bus (Redis/NATS), and enforce jittered backoff + slow-consumer eviction so one dead client never OOMs a node.

concept.whyItMatters: Collaborative editors, live trading tickers, multiplayer games, and AI token streaming require sub-50ms bidirectional push without HTTP header overhead. Naive WebSocket architectures collapse at 50k–100k connections due to per-socket memory, single-node state coupling, or thundering-herd reconnects during deploys.
whenToUse: True bidirectional, low-latency (<50ms) client-to-server and server-to-client messaging (chat, collaborative cursors, gaming, live bidding).
High-frequency updates (>1 msg/sec) where repeating HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 headers wastes bandwidth and battery.
Binary frame streaming (audio chunks, telemetry, protobuf deltas) over a single long-lived socket.
whenNotToUse: Server-to-client-only streaming like LLM token output or live feeds—Server-Sent Events (SSE) over HTTP/2 works with standard L7 proxies and auto-reconnects natively.
Infrequent notifications (a few times per hour)—use Web Push, FCM/APNs, or short polling to avoid holding idle TCP sockets.
Request/response CRUD APIs where stateless horizontal scaling, CDN caching, and standard HTTP status codes are simpler.
keyPoints: Each idle WebSocket consumes ~64–120 KB across kernel TCP buffers (sk_buff) and user-space runtime state; 1M concurrent sockets require ~64–120 GB RAM distributed across 16–32 gateway nodes.
A single backend IP:port pair hits the 65,535 ephemeral source-port ceiling when load-testing or proxying from one NAT IP; use multiple local IPs or L4 Direct Server Return (DSR).
WebSocket connections are stateful; scaling horizontally requires decoupling Connection Gateways from business services via a distributed pub/sub bus (NATS, Redis Pub/Sub, or Kafka).
TCP does not detect half-open dead clients immediately; gateways must send RFC 6455 Ping/Pong frames (opcodes 0x9/0xA) every 20–30s and close unresponsive sockets.
Rolling deploys of 100k+ connections trigger a thundering-herd reconnect storm (TLS handshakes + JWT auth) unless clients use randomized jittered exponential backoff.

examples.title: Live Financial Ticker & Order Book (2M Concurrent Sockets)
examples.scenario: A brokerage streams L2 order book deltas to 2M mobile/web clients during market open.
examples.outcome: AWS NLB (L4) distributes connections across 40 Rust/Go gateway pods (50k sockets/pod, SO_REUSEPORT); gateways subscribe to sharded NATS subjects and drop slow-consumer send queues after 500ms, holding p99 fan-out under 18ms.

examples.title: Multi-User Collaborative Canvas (Presence + CRDT)
examples.scenario: A design tool syncs cursor positions and CRDT operations across 500-user rooms.
examples.outcome: Consistent hashing routes rooms to sticky state workers while stateless Envoy/Netty edges terminate TLS and forward frames over gRPC streams, surviving edge restarts with <2s jittered reconnect.

tradeOffs.factor: L4 Load Balancer (NLB) vs. L7 Proxy (ALB/Envoy)
tradeOffs.pro: L4 NLB passes raw TCP with minimal memory overhead and supports millions of long-lived connections effortlessly.
tradeOffs.con: Cannot inspect HTTP paths/headers for routing or terminate TLS centrally, pushing TLS and auth into the gateway tier.

tradeOffs.pro: Redis Pub/Sub and core NATS deliver sub-millisecond fire-and-forget fan-out with zero disk overhead.
tradeOffs.con: Ephemeral delivery means messages sent during a 2-second client disconnect are lost unless paired with a replay log (Redis Streams/JetStream) keyed by sequence ID.

tradeOffs.factor: Per-Socket Read/Write Buffers vs. Epoll/Kqueue Event Loop
tradeOffs.pro: Event-driven async I/O (Netty, uWebSockets, Go netpoll) handles 50k–200k sockets per node without thread-per-connection stack bloat.
tradeOffs.con: Requires strict non-blocking handlers and bounded per-client outbound queues to avoid stalling the shared event loop.

failureModes.name: Reconnect Thundering Herd
failureModes.description: Deploying or restarting a gateway drops 50k connections simultaneously; every client immediately retries TLS + HTTP 101 + DB auth, overwhelming CPUs and auth stores.
failureModes.mitigation: Drain gateways gradually (e.g., 5% of sockets/sec with Close frame 1001) and enforce client-side jittered backoff: min(30s, 1s * 2^attempt) + rand(0, 2s).

failureModes.name: Slow-Consumer Memory Exhaustion (OOM)
failureModes.description: A mobile client on a stalled 3G link stops ACK-ing TCP packets while subscribed to a high-rate channel; the server's outbound send buffer grows until the gateway OOM-kills all 50k healthy clients.
failureModes.mitigation: Set strict per-connection outbound queue limits (e.g., 256 messages or 512 KB) and immediately close (`1008`/`1011`) or coalesce deltas for slow consumers.

failureModes.name: Hot-Room Pub/Sub Fan-Out Saturation
failureModes.description: A single celebrity livestream or global broadcast channel sends 1 msg/sec to 500k subscribers across 20 gateways, saturating Redis Pub/Sub single-threaded output buffers.
failureModes.mitigation: Shard hot channels across multiple pub/sub partitions or aggregate updates at the gateway so each gateway subscribes once per room rather than once per user.

failureModes.name: Silent Proxy Idle Timeout Drop
failureModes.description: Corporate NATs or cloud ALBs silently drop idle TCP flows after 60s without sending a FIN/RST, leaving client and server believing the socket is alive.
failureModes.mitigation: Send application/protocol Ping frames every 25s (well under the 60s NAT/ALB idle timeout) and terminate sockets that miss 2 consecutive Pongs.

commonMistakes: Storing room membership or session state in local gateway RAM, making horizontal scaling and rolling deploys impossible without dropping state.
Leaving Linux `ulimit -n` (max open file descriptors) at the default 1024 or 4096, causing `EMFILE` errors under load.
Authenticating only at the initial HTTP Upgrade without handling token expiration or revocation on connections that stay open for days.
Broadcasting unbatched per-keystroke/per-tick events instead of coalescing frames on a 16–50ms tick interval.
Neglecting sequence numbers (`seq_id`) on server-pushed events, forcing clients to refetch full state on every brief network blip.

sections.content:
## The idea

A WebSocket begins as a standard HTTP/1.1 `GET` request carrying `Upgrade: websocket`, `Connection: Upgrade`, and a base64 `Sec-WebSocket-Key`. When the server replies with **`101 Switching Protocols`**, the underlying TCP/TLS socket switches from HTTP request-response semantics to lightweight **RFC 6455 binary/text frames** (2–14 bytes of framing overhead per message).

Because the TCP connection stays pinned to a specific server process for minutes or hours, scaling WebSockets requires separating **stateful socket termination** (Connection Gateways) from **stateless business logic** via a distributed pub/sub backbone.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a message flow across a 1M-connection realtime platform:

1. **Handshake**: Client connects via `wss://rt.example.com/ws?token=...` through an L4 Load Balancer to Gateway Pod `gw-07`.
2. **Auth & Binding**: `gw-07` validates the short-lived JWT, registers `user_42 -> gw-07` in a fast presence store, and subscribes to `room:alpha` on the NATS/Redis pub/sub bus.
3. **Upstream Publish**: Client sends a 120-byte WebSocket frame; `gw-07` forwards it via gRPC to the stateless Chat/State Service, which persists the event with monotonic `seq_id=8841`.
4. **Fan-Out**: The service publishes `{room: "alpha", seq: 8841, payload}` to the pub/sub bus. Only gateways with active `room:alpha` subscribers (`gw-07`, `gw-12`) receive the message and write the framed bytes to their local `epoll` socket rings.
5. **Heartbeat & Backpressure**: Every 25s, `gw-07` sends a `0x9` Ping frame; if a client's outbound ring exceeds 512 KB, `gw-07` evicts the socket cleanly.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Kernel tuning, memory math, and port limits
sections.content:
## Kernel tuning, memory math, and port limits

Scaling beyond 50,000 connections per Linux host requires tuning both OS limits and memory budgets:

- **Memory Budget**: With `net.ipv4.tcp_rmem` and `tcp_wmem` tuned down (e.g., `4096 16384 65536`), kernel socket structures take ~20–32 KB per idle connection, plus ~30–60 KB in user-space (TLS session state + read/write buffers). That puts 1M connections at **~64–100 GB RAM**.
- **File Descriptors**: Raise `fs.file-max`, `fs.nr_open`, and systemd `LimitNOFILE=1048576`.
- **Ephemeral Port Exhaustion**: An outbound proxy connecting to a single backend `(dst_ip, dst_port)` is capped at ~28k–64k connections (`ip_local_port_range`). Bypass this by assigning multiple local source IPs on the proxy or terminating directly on L4-balanced gateway pods.

## Realtime transport protocols compared

| Protocol | Directionality | Framing & Overhead | Proxy / Firewall Traversal | Reconnect & Backpressure | Best Use Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **HTTP Long Polling** | Half-duplex | Full HTTP headers per poll | Universal (HTTP/1.1+) | Built-in via next poll; high server churn | Legacy fallback when WS is blocked |
| **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** | Server -> Client | UTF-8 text (`data: ...`), HTTP/2 multiplexed | Excellent over standard L7 proxies | Native `EventSource` `Last-Event-ID` | LLM token streaming, live feeds, tickers |
| **WebSocket (RFC 6455)** | Full-duplex | 2–14B binary/text frames | Good over TLS (`wss://443`); needs L7 `Upgrade` | Manual heartbeat + jittered backoff | Chat, collaborative apps, live trading |
| **WebTransport (HTTP/3)** | Full-duplex (multi-stream) | QUIC streams + unreliable datagrams | Requires UDP/443 (blocked on some corp nets) | Independent streams avoid TCP HoL blocking | Multiplayer games, ultra-low-latency media |

## Failure modes

- **TCP Head-of-Line (HoL) Blocking**: Because RFC 6455 runs over a single TCP stream, one lost packet stalls all multiplexed channels on that socket until retransmitted.
- **Unbounded Reconnect Loops**: Clients retrying on `1006 Abnormal Closure` without exponential backoff + jitter create self-inflicted DDoS outages whenever a regional AZ flaps.
- **Zombie Connections After Network Switch**: Mobile devices switching from Wi-Fi to 5G leave dead sockets open on the server until the next Ping timeout (25–50s), requiring `seq_id` replay on reconnect.

## Graceful draining and gapless replay

Zero-downtime deploys on stateful WebSocket fleets rely on **rate-limited draining** and **sequence replay**:

1. Remove the draining gateway pod from the load balancer target group so new handshakes stop.
2. Drip-close existing sockets at a capped rate (e.g., 1,000 sockets/sec) by sending WebSocket Close frame `1001 Going Away`, spreading the reconnect wave across 50 seconds instead of 1 millisecond.
3. When clients reconnect to a new pod, they pass `?since_seq=8841`; the gateway replays missed events from a short-lived Redis Stream / NATS JetStream ring buffer before resuming live pub/sub frames.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Tune `LimitNOFILE`, `somaxconn`, and `tcp_rmem`/`tcp_wmem` on gateway hosts for 50k–100k sockets/node.
- [ ] Enforce 25s Ping/Pong heartbeats and bounded per-client outbound queues (drop slow consumers cleanly).
- [ ] Implement jittered exponential backoff (`min(30s, 1s * 2^n) + rand(0, 2s)`) in all client SDKs.
- [ ] Drip-drain pods during rolling deploys (`1001 Going Away`) and support `since_seq` replay on reconnect.
- [ ] Monitor active connections, handshake rate/sec, outbound buffer drops, and pub/sub fan-out lag.

interviewProblems.title: WebSocket Real-Time Scaling
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on WebSocket Real-Time Scaling. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: WebSockets (RFC 6455) upgrade an HTTP connection into a persistent, full-duplex TCP frame stream; scaling to millions of concurrent connections shifts the bottleneck from request/sec to stateful memory, ephemeral ports, pub/sub fan-out, and reconnect storms.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Stateful WS Gateway Pool applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Pub/Sub + State Service.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Pub/Sub + State Service experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Drain gateways gradually (e.g., 5% of sockets/sec with Close frame 1001) and enforce client-side jittered backoff: min(30s, 1s * 2^attempt) + rand(0, 2s).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Terminate TLS and WebSockets on stateless L4-balanced connection gateways backed by a sharded pub/sub bus (Redis/NATS), and enforce jittered backoff + slow-consumer eviction so one dead client never OOMs a node.
Avoid trap: Storing room membership or session state in local gateway RAM, making horizontal scaling and rolling deploys impossible without dropping state.
Avoid trap: Leaving Linux `ulimit -n` (max open file descriptors) at the default 1024 or 4096, causing `EMFILE` errors under load.
When to reach for it: True bidirectional, low-latency (<50ms) client-to-server and server-to-client messaging (chat, collaborative cursors, gaming, live bidding).
When to reach for it: High-frequency updates (>1 msg/sec) where repeating HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 headers wastes bandwidth and battery.

putItTogether.title: Putting Websocket Realtime Scaling Together
putItTogether.summary: Terminate TLS and WebSockets on stateless L4-balanced connection gateways backed by a sharded pub/sub bus (Redis/NATS), and enforce jittered backoff + slow-consumer eviction so one dead client never OOMs a node.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Websocket Realtime Scaling before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: AWS NLB (L4) distributes connections across 40 Rust/Go gateway pods (50k sockets/pod, SO_REUSEPORT); gateways subscribe to sharded NATS subjects and drop slow-consumer send queues after 500ms, holding p99 fan-out under 18ms.
